identification.name: Tungsten Carbide - Cobalt (WC-6Co Cemented Carbide)
identification.common_form_notes: A true cermet (ceramic-metal composite): tungsten carbide grains bound by a 6 wt.% cobalt metal binder, powder-pressed and sintered to near-net shape. Supplied as blanks, rod, and finished inserts/wear parts rather than general machining stock. Machining requires diamond or CBN (cubic boron nitride) tooling and typically means grinding/EDM (electrical discharge machining), not conventional cutting — final precision grinding/lapping is standard for tooling and wear-part tolerances.
identification.notes: An extreme-property comparison material — not something a capstone team would machine or build with directly (requires specialized diamond-grinding/EDM equipment), included for hardness/density/stiffness comparison against the rest of the database. Flexural (transverse rupture) strength (1930 MPa) is recorded here as the tensile strength — this is standard practice for cemented carbides and other brittle ceramics/cermets, which cannot be reliably gripped and pulled in a simple tension test; it is not a true axial tensile strength. Shear strength is not derived via von Mises, unlike the ductile metals in this database — von Mises is a yield criterion for ductile materials undergoing plastic deformation, and cemented carbide fails by brittle fracture, so the criterion doesn't physically apply here. Hardness is reported on the Rockwell A scale (standard for cemented carbides given their extreme hardness — Rockwell B/C scales aren't appropriate). Shear modulus (259 GPa, not stored, listed by the source as "Calculated") is self-consistent with the stored E and ν: G = E/(2(1+ν)) = 627/2.42 ≈ 259 GPa, an exact match. Magnetic classification is Ferromagnetic, not Diamagnetic/Paramagnetic like other ceramics in this database — this is a genuine, well-known characteristic of cobalt-cemented carbides: the cobalt binder phase (6% by mass here) is itself ferromagnetic, and magnetic saturation measurement is a standard industrial QC (quality control) method for verifying binder content and detecting eta-phase (binder depletion) defects in cemented carbide grades. No melting point is stored — a WC-Co composite doesn't melt as a single phase (the cobalt binder melts around 1493°C; the WC ceramic phase itself doesn't melt but would decompose at much higher temperature), so a single "melting point" isn't a physically meaningful figure for the composite. Compressive strength and fracture toughness were not reported by this source and are left null rather than estimated — cemented carbides are known for very high compressive strength (often several GPa) and, unusually for a ceramic-hard material, decent fracture toughness (~8–15 MPa·m½) thanks to the metal binder phase, but no specific values were found here.

typical_usage: Cutting tool inserts, dies, punches, and wear-resistant parts (nozzles, seal faces, valve components) needing extreme hardness and wear resistance. A reference point for "how hard/dense/stiff can a practical engineering material get" — density nearly twice steel's, modulus roughly 3x steel's, but brittle and requiring specialized grinding/EDM to shape, unlike any metal in this database.
